$comment: Vectors for the amount_major transform (spec/03-manifest-dsl.md#field-transforms): converts a signed integer minor-unit amount to a major-unit decimal string, using the exponent for `currency` from exponents.json. amount_major is exact and involves no rounding: the exponent fixes the decimal point position, it never divides a value that doesn't land on it. Every runtime's amount_major implementation must match every case here byte-for-byte.

cases.description: Negative amount (refund/reversal): sign is preserved, never dropped
Amount under one major unit still pads to full exponent width
Zero-exponent currency: minor units equal major units, no decimal point
Three-decimal-place currency, sub-unit amount pads to full width
Largest positive int64 minor_units value (2^63 - 1), exponent 2
cases.why: A naive implementation that negates before checking for overflow, or that loses precision by round-tripping through a float64, will diverge from this exact value; see the int64-boundary case immediately below for the sharper edge.

cases.description: Smallest (most negative) int64 minor_units value (-2^63), exponent 2
cases.why: math.MinInt64 has no positive int64 representation of its own magnitude (2^63 does not fit in a signed 64-bit integer): an implementation that computes the absolute value as a naive `-minorUnits` overflows silently right back to the original negative value on this exact input, then either panics or produces a wrong sign/digits, depending on the language's overflow behaviour. This is the sharpest edge case in the whole Money model and the one most likely to be missed without an explicit vector for it.

cases.description: Three-decimal-place currency at a value requiring all three fractional digits, non-zero and non-round
